incidente.resumo: On January 31, 2017, GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours and lost database changes made between 17:20 and 23:30 UTC. Under high load, PostgreSQL replication broke and had to be rebuilt manually; during this, the primary's data directory was removed instead of the secondary's. Backups were not usable, and the service was restored from a 6-hour-old LVM snapshot copied from staging.

descricao.texto: The engineer noticed the removal was running on the primary and stopped it within a second or two, after about 300 GB had been removed.
trechos: The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

gatilho.texto: While trying to restore replication, the PostgreSQL data directory was wiped on the primary instead of the secondary.
trechos: Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary.
Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead.

descricao.texto: Increased load made the primary remove WAL segments before the secondary replicated them, breaking replication; rebuilding the secondary required manual, non-automated and poorly documented work, during which the wrong host was wiped.
trechos: The replication failed as WAL segments needed by the secondary were already removed from the primary.
Restoring this required manual work as this was not automated, nor was it documented properly.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: WAL archiving was not used, so the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually.
trechos: As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The pg_dump backups failed silently because they used PostgreSQL 9.2 against a 9.6 database.
trechos: This procedure failed silently because it was using PostgreSQL 9.2, while GitLab.com runs on PostgreSQL 9.6.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Backup failure emails were rejected because DMARC was not enabled for cronjob emails.
trechos: Unfortunately DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers.
trechos: While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: No one owned or regularly tested the backup procedure.
trechos: Because there was no ownership, as a result nobody was responsible for testing this procedure.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Restoring from staging was slow: copying data from staging to production took around 18 hours on throttled disks.
trechos: Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.

passos.texto: Chose the LVM snapshot taken 6 hours before the outage to minimize data loss.
trechos: To recover GitLab.com we decided to use the LVM snapshot created 6 hours before the outage

passos.texto: Copied the PostgreSQL data directory from staging to production.
trechos: Since copying over and restoring the data directory would be easier we decided to go with this solution.

passos.texto: Incremented all database sequences by 100,000 to avoid reusing IDs.
trechos: Increment all database sequences by 100,000 so one can't re-use IDs that might have been used before the outage.

passos.texto: Restored the database without webhooks on February 1 at 17:00 UTC.
trechos: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC we managed to restore the GitLab.com database without webhooks.

passos.texto: Restored webhooks from a separate staging database and confirmed operation around 18:00 UTC.
trechos: Restoring webhooks was done by creating a separate staging database using the LVM snapshot, but without triggering the removal of webhooks.
Around 18:00 UTC we finished the final restoration procedures such as restoring the webhooks and confirming everything was operating as expected.

acoes.texto: Make the shell prompt clearly differentiate hosts and environments.
trechos: Update PS1 across all hosts to more clearly differentiate between hosts and environments (#1094)
Prometheus monitoring for backups (#1095)

acoes.texto: Take hourly LVM snapshots of production databases.
trechos: Hourly LVM snapshots of the production databases (#1098)

acoes.texto: Automate testing of PostgreSQL backup restores.
trechos: Automated testing of recovering PostgreSQL database backups (#1102)

acoes.texto: Improve PostgreSQL replication documentation and runbooks.
trechos: Improve PostgreSQL replication documentation/runbooks (#1103)

acoes.texto: Assign an owner for data durability.
trechos: Assign an owner for data durability

acoes.texto: Improve the abuse reporting and response system.
trechos: Finally, we're looking into improving our abuse reporting and response system.
GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours.
